We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
papers.research_question: Is causal abstraction sufficient for mechanistic interpretability when alignment maps are not constrained to be linear?
papers.core_contribution: Causal abstraction becomes vacuous when alignment maps are allowed to be arbitrarily complex, leading to the non-linear representation dilemma where there is no principled way to balance map complexity and accuracy.
papers.conclusion: Causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability without assumptions about how models encode information.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretically, any algorithm can be perfectly mapped to any neural network under reasonable assumptions if alignment maps are arbitrarily complex.
Empirically, non-linear alignment maps can achieve near-perfect interchange intervention accuracy even on randomly initialized models that do not solve the task.
The complexity of alignment maps needed to achieve perfect IIA decreases as the model trains.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical result relies on assumptions such as input-injectivity and output-surjectivity of the neural network.
Empirical alignment map training can suffer from grokking and requires careful hyperparameter tuning.
future_direction: Studying the connection between information-encoding assumptions and causal abstraction.
papers.abstract: The concept of causal abstraction got recently popularised to demystify the opaque decision-making processes of machine learning models; in short, a neural network can be abstracted as a higher-level algorithm if there exists a function which allows us to map between them. Notably, most interpretability papers implement these maps as linear functions, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis: the idea that features are encoded linearly in a model's representations. However, this linearity constraint is not required by the definition of causal abstraction. In this work, we critically examine the concept of causal abstraction by considering arbitrarily powerful alignment maps. In particular, we prove that under reasonable assumptions, any neural network can be mapped to any algorithm, rendering this unrestricted notion of causal abstraction trivial and uninformative. We complement these theoretical findings with empirical evidence, demonstrating that it is possible to perfectly map models to algorithms even when these models are incapable of solving the actual task; e.g., on an experiment using randomly initialised language models, our alignment maps reach 100\% interchange-intervention accuracy on the indirect object identification task. This raises the non-linear representation dilemma: if we lift the linearity constraint imposed to alignment maps in causal abstraction analyses, we are left with no principled way to balance the inherent trade-off between these maps' complexity and accuracy. Together, these results suggest an answer to our title's question: causal abstraction is not enough for mechanistic interpretability, as it becomes vacuous without assumptions about how models encode information. Studying the connection between this information-encoding assumption and causal abstraction should lead to exciting future work.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: A Mathematical Philosophy of Explanations in Mechanistic Interpretability -- The Strange Science Part I.i
papers.research_question: What is the nature of explanations in mechanistic interpretability? How can we define mechanistic interpretability and what are its inherent limits?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a philosophical framework for mechanistic interpretability, including the Explanatory View Hypothesis, a definition of mechanistic interpretability as producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations, and the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that if the Principle of Explanatory Optimism holds, interpretability could enable humans to understand machine knowledge, making it a crucial scientific endeavor for the future of human understanding.
papers.key_findings:
The Explanatory View Hypothesis posits that neural networks contain implicit explanations of their behavior that can be extracted and understood.
Explanatory Faithfulness is defined as the extent to which an explanation matches the model's internal ur-explanations, and is well-defined under the Explanatory View.
Mechanistic Interpretability is defined as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks.
Mechanistic Interpretability has inherent limits, such as theory-ladenness and the potential for high explanatory complexity that may make models incomprehensible to humans.
The Principle of Explanatory Optimism, which states that the algorithmic structure of generalizing neural networks is human-understandable, is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability may be limited by the theory-ladenness of observations, where the interpreter's prior theories influence what they can discover.
There is a risk that the explanatory complexity of models might be too high for humans to understand, which would make mechanistic interpretability intractable.
future_direction: Formalize the conjectures of Strong and Weak Explanatory Optimism, including defining explanatory complexity classes and explanatory universality.
Prove the formalized conjectures to assess the truth value of the Principle of Explanatory Optimism.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability aims to understand neural networks through causal explanations. We argue for the Explanatory View Hypothesis: that Mechanistic Interpretability research is a principled approach to understanding models because neural networks contain implicit explanations which can be extracted and understood. We hence show that Explanatory Faithfulness, an assessment of how well an explanation fits a model, is well-defined. We propose a definition of Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) as the practice of producing Model-level, Ontic, Causal-Mechanistic, and Falsifiable explanations of neural networks, allowing us to distinguish MI from other interpretability paradigms and detail MI's inherent limits. We formulate the Principle of Explanatory Optimism, a conjecture which we argue is a necessary precondition for the success of Mechanistic Interpretability.

papers.title: Learning biologically relevant features in a pathology foundation model using sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from the embeddings of a pathology foundation model, and how do these features evolve across model layers and generalize across domains?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can extract monosemantic, biologically interpretable features from a pathology foundation model's embeddings, revealing that these features evolve across layers (from low-level color to high-level cell-type concepts) and are robust to domain shifts like scanner and stain type.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders enable the extraction of interpretable, monosemantic, and biologically-grounded features from a pathology foundation model, demonstrating the model's internal representations evolve to capture robust biological concepts, which motivates further work on explainable features for medical applications.
papers.key_findings:
Individual SAE dimensions show strong correlations with counts of specific cell types (e.g., plasma cells, lymphocytes), demonstrating monosemantic representation of biological concepts.
These biologically-grounded SAE features are unique to the pathology-pretrained model (PLUTO) and are not found in a self-supervised model (DINO) pretrained on natural images.
SAE features evolve across the model's depth: early layers correlate with low-level color features, while later layers correlate with high-level cell-type features, indicating the model gains invariance to spurious factors.
The monosemantic SAE representations (e.g., for plasma cells) are robust and generalizable to out-of-domain pathology datasets (CPTAC).
Cell-type specific SAE dimensions identified in later layers show reduced sensitivity to scanner and stain variations, indicating the model learns robust biological representations.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was restricted to a vanilla sparse autoencoder; newer variations like gated SAE and k-sparse SAE were not applied.
The findings are based on a single pathology foundation model (PLUTO); translation to other pathology foundation models is left for future study.
Interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features were not performed.
future_direction: Application of newer sparse autoencoder variations (e.g., gated SAE, k-sparse SAE) in pathology.
Analysis of how the findings translate to other pathology foundation models.
Performing interventions in the SAE latent space to characterize impact on robustness to spurious features.
papers.abstract: Pathology plays an important role in disease diagnosis, treatment decision-making and drug development. Previous works on interpretability for machine learning models on pathology images have revolved around methods such as attention value visualization and deriving human-interpretable features from model heatmaps. Mechanistic interpretability is an emerging area of model interpretability that focuses on reverse-engineering neural networks. Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising direction in terms of extracting monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations. In this work, we trained a Sparse Autoencoder on the embeddings of a pathology pretrained foundation model. We found that Sparse Autoencoder features represent interpretable and monosemantic biological concepts. In particular, individual SAE dimensions showed strong correlations with cell type counts such as plasma cells and lymphocytes. These biological representations were unique to the pathology pretrained model and were not found in a self-supervised model pretrained on natural images. We demonstrated that such biologically-grounded monosemantic representations evolved across the model's depth, and the pathology foundation model eventually gained robustness to non-biological factors such as scanner type. The emergence of biologically relevant SAE features was generalizable to an out-of-domain dataset. Our work paves the way for further exploration around interpretable feature dimensions and their utility for medical and clinical applications.

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: Beyond Label Attention: Transparency in Language Models for Automated Medical Coding via Dictionary Learning
papers.research_question: How can dictionary learning be used to improve the interpretability of medical coding language models beyond label attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AutoCodeDL, a method that combines dictionary learning with label attention to provide more interpretable, dictionary-based rationales for ICD code predictions in medical language models.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that combining dictionary learning with label attention improves interpretability for medical coding models, providing a dictionary-based rationale for predictions and laying groundwork for future healthcare interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Dictionary learning can uncover hidden medical meanings in token embeddings, explaining why label attention highlights seemingly irrelevant tokens like stop words.
AutoCodeDL provides more precise explanations than label attention alone, as shown by a higher ratio of target code probability drop to non-target changes after ablation.
Learned dictionary features can steer model behavior, changing predictions for specific subsets of ICD codes without modifying model weights.
The dictionary features are human interpretable, demonstrating coherence and distinctiveness in automated and human evaluations.
Sparse autoencoders (L1 and SPINE) outperform baseline unsupervised methods in explainability and hidden meaning identification.
papers.limitation:
Sparse autoencoders cannot perfectly reconstruct PLM embeddings and thus cannot fully capture a model's downstream performance.
There exist dead or missing features in the dictionary, indicating not all features are useful or interpretable.
The sparse dictionaries learned are not as coherent as supervised mappings like LAAT, limiting human understandability.
Interpreting only the last layer PLM embeddings is insufficient for fully capturing and interpreting a PLM's behavior.
The resolution of dictionary features is lacking compared to the granularity of medical codes, suggesting features represent higher abstract concepts rather than highly-specific codes.
The applicability of scaling sparse autoencoders to smaller scale language datasets is unknown.
future_direction: Exploring more expressive representation learning techniques like causal and disentanglement methods for interpretability gains.
Unraveling complex relationships within medical PLMs through automated circuit discovery combined with dictionary learning.
Scaling up sparse autoencoders to potentially millions of dictionary features for extremely large language models.
papers.abstract: Medical coding, the translation of unstructured clinical text into standardized medical codes, is a crucial but time-consuming healthcare practice. Though large language models (LLM) could automate the coding process and improve the efficiency of such tasks, interpretability remains paramount for maintaining patient trust. Current efforts in interpretability of medical coding applications rely heavily on label attention mechanisms, which often leads to the highlighting of extraneous tokens irrelevant to the ICD code. To facilitate accurate interpretability in medical language models, this paper leverages dictionary learning that can efficiently extract sparsely activated representations from dense language model embeddings in superposition. Compared with common label attention mechanisms, our model goes beyond token-level representations by building an interpretable dictionary which enhances the mechanistic-based explanations for each ICD code prediction, even when the highlighted tokens are medically irrelevant. We show that dictionary features can steer model behavior, elucidate the hidden meanings of upwards of 90% of medically irrelevant tokens, and are human interpretable.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of LLMs in Finance
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability techniques be applied to understand and control the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) in financial applications to improve transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates the application of mechanistic interpretability techniques—Logit Lens, Attribution Patching, and Sparse Autoencoders—to financial use cases, showing how they can be used to understand, debug, and steer model behavior for tasks like sentiment analysis, bias detection, and hallucination reduction.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability offers a promising path to dissect and guide AI-driven financial decisions with greater transparency and control, though challenges in scalability, generalization, and mapping abstract features to human-understandable concepts remain.
papers.key_findings:
Logit Lens analysis reveals how token prediction probabilities evolve across transformer layers in response to financial prompts, showing refinement of predictions in deeper layers.
Attribution Patching identifies specific attention heads in layers 8 and 10 of GPT-2 as causally significant for correct financial predictions.
Sparse Autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from model activations relevant to financial concepts like credit risk.
Feature steering via Sparse Autoencoders can modify model outputs, such as improving sentiment classification accuracy for credit risk analysis without fine-tuning.
A feature-activation-thresholded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach can reduce hallucinations in financial question-answering by ensuring external factual data is incorporated when internal feature activations are low.
papers.limitation:
Scalability is a major concern, as manual circuit analysis becomes infeasible for very large models, and automated interpretability tools are still in early development.
Many techniques fail to generalize effectively to real-world financial applications, as models often rely on abstract representations not directly mappable to human-understandable financial concepts.
The evolving nature of financial markets and regulations means models trained on historical data may struggle to adapt, requiring dynamic interpretability pipelines.
Identifying a particular neuron or attention head does not always clarify the exact influence of features such as credit score or volatility on the final decision.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability with feature-level attributions to ensure AI decisions are explainable in terms of real-world financial indicators.
Developing a hybrid approach that integrates traditional statistical modeling techniques using financial time series data with unstructured data processed by LLMs.
Building fully integrated interpretability tooling that combines techniques from various research efforts to streamline analysis workflows for financial professionals.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a spectrum of tasks in financial services, including report generation, chatbots, sentiment analysis, regulatory compliance, investment advisory, financial knowledge retrieval, and summarization. However, their intrinsic complexity and lack of transparency pose significant challenges, especially in the highly regulated financial sector, where interpretability, fairness, and accountability are critical. As far as we are aware, this paper presents the first application in the finance domain of understanding and utilizing the inner workings of LLMs through mechanistic interpretability, addressing the pressing need for transparency and control in AI systems. Mechanistic interpretability is the most intuitive and transparent way to understand LLM behavior by reverse-engineering their internal workings. By dissecting the activations and circuits within these models, it provides insights into how specific features or components influence predictions - making it possible not only to observe but also to modify model behavior. In this paper, we explore the theoretical aspects of mechanistic interpretability and demonstrate its practical relevance through a range of financial use cases and experiments, including applications in trading strategies, sentiment analysis, bias, and hallucination detection. While not yet widely adopted, mechanistic interpretability is expected to become increasingly vital as adoption of LLMs increases. Advanced interpretability tools can ensure AI systems remain ethical, transparent, and aligned with evolving financial regulations. In this paper, we have put special emphasis on how these techniques can help unlock interpretability requirements for regulatory and compliance purposes - addressing both current needs and anticipating future expectations from financial regulators globally.

papers.title: HyperDAS: Towards Automating Mechanistic Interpretability with Hypernetworks
papers.research_question: How can we automate the process of identifying features in hidden representations that mediate concepts, avoiding brute-force search?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces HyperDAS, a hypernetwork-based method that automates the search for concept features in hidden representations, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the RA VEL benchmark.
papers.conclusion: HyperDAS is a novel approach that advances interpretability by automating causal interpretability work and achieving state-of-the-art performance.
papers.key_findings:
HyperDAS outperforms the previous state-of-the-art (MDAS) on the RA VEL benchmark.
HyperDAS automatically selects token positions for intervention, often selecting multiple tokens (53% of the time).
HyperDAS requires more compute than MDAS but is more memory efficient when dealing with multiple attributes.
The learned Householder vectors for different attributes form clusters, indicating distinct subspaces for different attributes.
Intervention location varies across layers: early layers target random tokens, middle layers target entity tokens, and deeper layers target syntax tokens.
papers.limitation:
HyperDAS assumes the target concept is mediated by linear features, but non-linear mediators are a possibility.
Applying supervised machine learning to interpretability has the potential to lead to false positive results (injecting new information rather than faithfully interpreting the model).
future_direction: Explore non-linear mediators.
Further investigate the balance between uncovering latent causal relationships and the risk of model steering.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability has made great strides in identifying neural network features (e.g., directions in hidden activation space) that mediate concepts(e.g., the birth year of a person) and enable predictable manipulation. Distributed alignment search (DAS) leverages supervision from counterfactual data to learn concept features within hidden states, but DAS assumes we can afford to conduct a brute force search over potential feature locations. To address this, we present HyperDAS, a transformer-based hypernetwork architecture that (1) automatically locates the token-positions of the residual stream that a concept is realized in and (2) constructs features of those residual stream vectors for the concept. In experiments with Llama3-8B, HyperDAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on the RAVEL benchmark for disentangling concepts in hidden states. In addition, we review the design decisions we made to mitigate the concern that HyperDAS (like all powerful interpretabilty methods) might inject new information into the target model rather than faithfully interpreting it.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks? What model components are responsible for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Language models process arithmetic queries by transferring operand and operator information from early layers to the last token via attention, and then late MLP modules generate result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Causal mediation analysis reveals the mechanistic process of arithmetic reasoning in LMs, suggesting avenues for model pruning and targeted training.
papers.key_findings:
The model conveys operand and operator information from early layers to the last token using attention mechanisms.
Late MLP modules at the last token incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
The activation patterns are specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
The relative importance of late MLPs is high for arithmetic but low for other tasks.
Neuron-level interventions show that the top neurons for arithmetic overlap partially with number retrieval and not more than random with factual knowledge.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators.
The queries are synthetically generated and not from real-life math word problems.
The analysis does not break down attention into individual heads.
future_direction: Study a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expand analysis to real-life math word problems.
Identify specific attention heads responsible for forwarding information.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Interpretability machine learning models: A critical analysis of techniques and applications
papers.research_question: What are the various techniques and applications of interpretable machine learning models, and what are their strengths and limitations?
papers.core_contribution: A critical review of interpretable machine learning techniques and their applications, highlighting strengths, limitations, and future directions.
papers.conclusion: Interpretable machine learning is essential for transparency and accountability, with future trends emphasizing proactive decision-making, integration with technologies like IoT, and a focus on ethics and fairness.
papers.key_findings:
Traditional linear models are interpretable but may not capture complex relationships in modern datasets.
Model-agnostic techniques like LIME and SHAP provide post-hoc interpretability but may face challenges in faithfully representing model decision boundaries.
Interpretable models are crucial in critical domains like healthcare and finance for gaining trust and ensuring accountability.
There is an interpretability-accuracy trade-off that needs to be considered when selecting models.
Future applications will focus on proactive decision-making, integration with emerging technologies, and ethical considerations.
papers.limitation:
Interpretability-accuracy trade-off in model selection.
Lack of standardized evaluation metrics for interpretability.
future_direction: Integration of domain knowledge into interpretable models
Incorporation of interpretability as an integral part of the model development process
Emphasis on transparency, fairness, and accountability in algorithmic decision-making
papers.abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of machine learning, the demand for interpretable models has become paramount to ensure transparency, accountability, and user trust. This review paper critically examines various techniques and applications associated with interpretable machine learning models. The burgeoning complexity of black-box models, such as deep neural networks, has underscored the need for understanding and explaining model decisions, especially in domains where critical decisions impact human lives, such as healthcare, finance, and criminal justice. The paper begins by exploring the motivations behind the surge in interest in interpretable machine learning, elucidating the challenges posed by inherently opaque models. Subsequently, it provides an in-depth analysis of popular interpretable model techniques, ranging from traditional linear models to modern approaches like LIME (Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations) and SHAP (SHapley Additive ex Planations). By dissecting the strengths and limitations of each technique, the paper aims to empower practitioners and researchers to make informed choices based on their specific use cases and requirements. Furthermore, the review delves into real-world applications where interpretable models play a pivotal role. Examples include healthcare diagnostics, where the interpretability of a model's decisions is crucial for gaining the trust of medical professionals and ensuring patient safety. Similarly, in the financial sector, interpretable models aid in risk assessment and regulatory compliance. The paper critically examines these applications, shedding light on instances where interpretable models offer tangible benefits over their opaque counterparts. The review also addresses the ongoing challenges in the field, such as the interpretability-accuracy trade-off and the need for standardized evaluation metrics. It emphasizes the importance of developing universally accepted benchmarks to objectively assess the interpretability of different models. Moreover, the paper discusses emerging trends and future directions in interpretable machine learning, including the integration of domain knowledge and the incorporation of interpretability as an integral part of the model development process.

papers.title: Integrating Deep Learning and Interpretable Regression Models for Transparent Decision Support in Healthcare Diagnostics
papers.research_question: How can deep learning and interpretable regression models be integrated to achieve transparent decision support in healthcare diagnostics while maintaining predictive performance?
papers.core_contribution: This study demonstrates that a hybrid framework integrating deep learning embeddings with interpretable regression models can achieve competitive predictive performance while providing transparent, clinically interpretable explanations for healthcare diagnostics.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid approach bridges the gap between predictive accuracy and explainability, offering a viable pathway for transparent AI in healthcare diagnostics, though limitations include static data and approximate explanations.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model (Logistic Regression on embeddings) achieved AUC=0.9829 and high sensitivity, balancing performance and interpretability.
SHAP analysis revealed that clinical variables like age, creatinine, and blood pressure were top contributors to predictions, aligning with medical knowledge.
The deep model's embeddings captured complex physiological patterns, enabling effective use in interpretable regression.
Baseline logistic regression on raw features showed perfect scores on test data, indicating potential overfitting or data leakage.
The framework provides both global and local explanations through coefficients and SHAP values.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was constrained to static, tabular representations of patient data, excluding temporal dynamics.
Interpretability is limited to feature-level attributions and linear coefficients, which are descriptive rather than causal.
SHAP approximations can be sensitive to background distribution and assume feature independence, potentially leading to misleading attributions.
Mapping from embeddings to raw features is inherently approximate and may not provide stable interpretations.
Generalizability concerns due to dataset from a single medical center and potential data leakage.
future_direction: Incorporate temporal modeling using LSTMs or Transformers to capture sequential patient data.
Extend the framework to multi-class and multi-label diagnostic outcomes.
Integrate causal interpretability and counterfactual reasoning for actionable insights.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have demonstrated exceptional predictive capabilities in healthcare diagnostics, yet their black-box nature limits clinical adoption due to a lack of interpretability and trust. This study addresses this limitation by developing a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates deep representation learning with interpretable regression modeling. Using the MIMIC-IV dataset, sourced from U.S. intensive care units, and comprising patient demographics, vital signs, and laboratory data, we train a deep neural network to learn 128-dimensional patient embeddings that capture underlying physiological patterns. These embeddings are then used as inputs to interpretable regression models, Logistic Regression, and Generalized Additive Models, to predict hospital mortality while maintaining transparency. SHAP-based interpretability analysis is employed to quantify and visualize the contribution of each embedding dimension and clinical feature to model predictions. Experimental results show that the hybrid model achieves competitive performance relative to standalone deep models, while providing clear feature-level explanations through regression coefficients and SHAP importance rankings. The findings demonstrate that deep–deep-interpretable hybrid architectures can bridge the performance–explainability divide, offering a viable pathway for deploying transparent, trustworthy AI systems in clinical diagnostics. This integration not only enhances predictive reliability but also strengthens clinician confidence through evidence-based, interpretable decision support.

papers.title: It's FLAN time! Summing feature-wise latent representations for interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we build interpretable deep learning models that retain the representational power of neural networks while being interpretable by design?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FLANs, a class of structurally constrained neural networks that are interpretable by design, achieving reasonable performance on complex datasets without needing post-hoc interpretation methods.
papers.conclusion: FLANs are a powerful and interpretable model class that can be natively interpreted without post-hoc methods, representing an important step towards interpretable machine learning in complex domains.
papers.key_findings:
FLANs achieve comparable performance to established models on a series of benchmark datasets across tabular, image, and text domains.
FLANs provide native interpretability through feature importance (via latent norms) and example-based explanations without the need for post-hoc methods.
FLANs may have difficulties in learning complex/long interactions, as seen in the CUB and IMDb datasets, but can still achieve 100% training accuracy, indicating the ability to learn complex interactions that may not generalize.
papers.limitation: FLANs may have difficulties in learning complex/long interactions, as seen in the CUB and IMDb datasets.
future_direction: Address the generalization difficulties of the model.
Run user studies to further validate the interpretability of the model.
papers.abstract: Interpretability has become a necessary feature for machine learning models deployed in critical scenarios, e.g. legal system, healthcare. In these situations, algorithmic decisions may have (potentially negative) long-lasting effects on the end-user affected by the decision. In many cases, the representational power of deep learning models is not needed, therefore simple and interpretable models (e.g. linear models) should be preferred. However, in high-dimensional and/or complex domains (e.g. computer vision), the universal approximation capabilities of neural networks are required. Inspired by linear models and the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem, we propose a novel class of structurally-constrained neural networks, which we call FLANs (Feature-wise Latent Additive Networks). Crucially, FLANs process each input feature separately, computing for each of them a representation in a common latent space. These feature-wise latent representations are then simply summed, and the aggregated representation is used for prediction. These constraints (which are at the core of the interpretability of linear models) allow a user to estimate the effect of each individual feature independently from the others, enhancing interpretability. In a set of experiments across different domains, we show how without compromising excessively the test performance, the structural constraints proposed in FLANs indeed facilitates the interpretability of deep learning models. We quantitatively compare FLANs interpretability to post-hoc methods using recently introduced metrics, discussing the advantages of natively interpretable models over a post-hoc analysis.

papers.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the interpretability of latent representations in CNNs by measuring the alignment between individual hidden units and semantic concepts, and what factors affect this interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Network Dissection, a framework for quantifying the interpretability of CNN representations by evaluating the alignment between individual convolutional units and a broad set of semantic concepts, and uses it to show interpretability is an axis-aligned property affected by architecture, training data, and regularization.
papers.conclusion: Network Dissection provides a method to quantify interpretability in CNNs, revealing that interpretability is an axis-aligned property indicative of partially disentangled representations, and is influenced by network architecture, training data, and training techniques.
papers.key_findings:
Interpretability of units is not axis-independent; random rotations of the representation significantly reduce the number of unique concept detectors, indicating interpretability is a special alignment learned by the network.
Deeper network architectures (ResNet > VGG > GoogLeNet > AlexNet) and training on scene-centric data (Places) lead to more interpretable units (more unique concept detectors).
Self-supervised training tasks produce fewer object detectors and more texture detectors compared to supervised training, and the form of self-supervision (e.g., colorization) affects which concepts emerge.
Batch normalization significantly reduces interpretability, while dropout and different random initializations have less impact on the final level of interpretability.
Widening a convolutional layer (increasing the number of units) can increase the number of unique concept detectors without significantly harming classification accuracy.
papers.limitation: Network dissection works only as well as the underlying dataset; if a unit matches a human-understandable concept that is absent in Broden, it will not score well for interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the Broden dataset to include more kinds of visual concepts.
Finding ways to capture the benefits of batch normalization without destroying interpretability.
papers.abstract: We propose a general framework called Network Dissection for quantifying the interpretability of latent representations of CNNs by evaluating the alignment between individual hidden units and a set of semantic concepts. Given any CNN model, the proposed method draws on a data set of concepts to score the semantics of hidden units at each intermediate convolutional layer. The units with semantics are labeled across a broad range of visual concepts including objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors. We use the proposed method to test the hypothesis that interpretability is an axis-independent property of the representation space, then we apply the method to compare the latent representations of various networks when trained to solve different classification problems. We further analyze the effect of training iterations, compare networks trained with different initializations, and measure the effect of dropout and batch normalization on the interpretability of deep visual representations. We demonstrate that the proposed method can shed light on characteristics of CNN models and training methods that go beyond measurements of their discriminative power.

papers.title: Mapping Knowledge Representations to Concepts: A Review and New Perspectives
papers.research_question: How do current methods extract internal knowledge representations in a neural network and map them to human-understandable concepts? Can Deductive-Nomological (D-N) explanation taxonomy and causal types of explanations be useful in order to analyse what can be expected, and not expected, from knowledge representations in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a targeted review of research that aims to associate internal neural network representations with human understandable concepts, and proposes using Deductive-Nomological explanations and theories of causality as a taxonomy to understand the capabilities and limitations of such explanations.
papers.conclusion: The review raises important questions about the goal of explanations and the type of knowledge extractable from neural networks, emphasizing the need to differentiate between understanding the trained model and providing actionable decisions. It argues for involving users to emphasize contextual dependence and refocus research on the limitations of ML systems.
papers.key_findings:
Methods for extracting knowledge representations are dominated by two approaches: Feature Based Attribution (FBA) for local understanding and Internal Knowledge Representation (IKR) extraction for global understanding.
There is an ambiguity in the goal of model explainability: understanding the ML model versus providing actionable explanations in the deployment domain.
The reviewed research lacks user studies, despite heavy reliance on human abilities to compare images and infer concepts.
Explanations that aim for intervention or counterfactual reasoning rely on causal relations, but these are only valid for the ML model in isolation and not necessarily for the real-world domain.
The Deductive-Nomological explanation taxonomy is found useful for analyzing what can be expected from neural network explanations, highlighting that current methods typically aim for kind-data or model-data relations, not theory-data or entity-data relations.
papers.limitation:
The choice to use the D-N model and Overton's schematic overview delimits the type of explanations aimed for and excludes pragmatic, inductive statistical, teleological, and historical explanations.
The understanding of the concept 'concept' is not well-grounded from an ontological and epistemological perspective.
future_direction: Conducting user studies that actively involve users to emphasize contextual dependence.
Combining IKR and FBA methods in studies aiming for a global meta-perspective of model understanding.

Using scientific explanations and theories to formulate falsifiable hypotheses and evaluate how well a trained ML model models the usage domain, moving beyond the idea that more data solves the problem of induction.
papers.abstract: The success of neural networks builds to a large extent on their ability to create internal knowledge representations from real-world high-dimensional data, such as images, sound, or text. Approaches to extract and present these representations, in order to explain the neural network's decisions, is an active and multifaceted research field. To gain a deeper understanding of a central aspect of this field, we have performed a targeted review focusing on research that aims to associate internal representations with human understandable concepts. In doing this, we added a perspective on the existing research by using primarily deductive nomological explanations as a proposed taxonomy. We find this taxonomy and theories of causality, useful for understanding what can be expected, and not expected, from neural network explanations. The analysis additionally uncovers an ambiguity in the reviewed literature related to the goal of model explainability; is it understanding the ML model or, is it actionable explanations useful in the deployment domain?

papers.title: XAI-MeD: Explainable Knowledge Guided Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Domain Generalization and Rare Class Detection in Medical Imaging
papers.research_question: How to improve robustness under distribution shift, enhance rare-class sensitivity, and provide transparent interpretations in medical AI by integrating expert knowledge with deep learning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces XAI-MeD, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates clinical expert knowledge with deep learning to improve domain generalization, rare-class detection, and provide interpretable explanations in medical imaging.
papers.conclusion: XAI-MeD represents a significant step toward human-centered AI by integrating neural and symbolic paradigms, ensuring robustness, interpretability, and clinical alignment in medical AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
XAI-MeD achieves 84.6% accuracy and 89.7% sensitivity in SOZ localization, outperforming standalone DL and knowledge baselines.
The framework reduces manual expert review effort by 84.2% in SOZ localization.
In DR grading, XAI-MeD improves F1-scores for rare classes by over 10% compared to standalone DL.
XAI-MeD demonstrates robust cross-domain generalization, with 6% gain in accuracy on unseen datasets.
Ablation studies show that neuro-symbolic fusion achieves the best generalization performance.
papers.limitation:
Dependence on auxiliary supervised models (e.g., YOLO lesion detectors and U-Net anatomical segmenters) which require manually annotated data.
Finite clinical knowledge coverage due to reliance on expert-defined rule sets, unable to capture rare or edge cases not in training.
future_direction: Exploring weakly supervised or self-supervised lesion discovery to reduce dependency on manual annotations.
Investigating rule induction from large medical corpora using large language models to expand knowledge coverage.
papers.abstract: Explainability domain generalization and rare class reliability are critical challenges in medical AI where deep models often fail under real world distribution shifts and exhibit bias against infrequent clinical conditions This paper introduces XAIMeD an explainable medical AI framework that integrates clinically accurate expert knowledge into deep learning through a unified neuro symbolic architecture XAIMeD is designed to improve robustness under distribution shift enhance rare class sensitivity and deliver transparent clinically aligned interpretations The framework encodes clinical expertise as logical connectives over atomic medical propositions transforming them into machine checkable class specific rules Their diagnostic utility is quantified through weighted feature satisfaction scores enabling a symbolic reasoning branch that complements neural predictions A confidence weighted fusion integrates symbolic and deep outputs while a Hunt inspired adaptive routing mechanism guided by Entropy Imbalance Gain EIG and Rare Class Gini mitigates class imbalance high intra class variability and uncertainty We evaluate XAIMeD across diverse modalities on four challenging tasks i Seizure Onset Zone SOZ localization from rs fMRI ii Diabetic Retinopathy grading across 6 multicenter datasets demonstrate substantial performance improvements including 6 percent gains in cross domain generalization and a 10 percent improved rare class F1 score far outperforming state of the art deep learning baselines Ablation studies confirm that the clinically grounded symbolic components act as effective regularizers ensuring robustness to distribution shifts XAIMeD thus provides a principled clinically faithful and interpretable approach to multimodal medical AI.

papers.title: On the definition and importance of interpretability in scientific machine learning
papers.research_question: What is interpretability in the context of scientific machine learning, and how does interpretability advance scientific knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a definition of interpretability for scientific machine learning that emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity, and questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by proposing a definition of interpretability focused on physical meaning, and argues that interpretability is useful in science as a tool for unification, with sparsity facilitating derivation from fundamental principles.
papers.key_findings:
Researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability.
Existing definitions and methods from the broader interpretable ML literature are inadequate for scientific machine learning.
Interpretability in science should be defined as understanding the physical meaning or mechanism of an equation, not merely its mathematical sparsity.
Sparsity is neither necessary nor sufficient for interpretability in science; prior knowledge is required to connect sparse equations to underlying principles.
Interpretability advances scientific knowledge by unifying disparate phenomena under a small set of fundamental physical principles.
future_direction: Future work will explore whether interpretations can be extracted from recovered equations when relevant prior knowledge is lacking.
papers.abstract: Though neural networks trained on large datasets have been successfully used to describe and predict many physical phenomena, there is a sense among scientists that, unlike traditional scientific models comprising simple mathematical expressions, their findings cannot be integrated into the body of scientific knowledge. Critics of machine learning's inability to produce human-understandable relationships have converged on the concept of "interpretability" as its point of departure from more traditional forms of science. As the growing interest in interpretability has shown, researchers in the physical sciences seek not just predictive models, but also to uncover the fundamental principles that govern a system of interest. However, clarity around a definition of interpretability and the precise role that it plays in science is lacking in the literature. In this work, we argue that researchers in equation discovery and symbolic regression tend to conflate the concept of sparsity with interpretability. We review key papers on interpretable machine learning from outside the scientific community and argue that, though the definitions and methods they propose can inform questions of interpretability for scientific machine learning (SciML), they are inadequate for this new purpose. Noting these deficiencies, we propose an operational definition of interpretability for the physical sciences. Our notion of interpretability emphasizes understanding of the mechanism over mathematical sparsity. Innocuous though it may seem, this emphasis on mechanism shows that sparsity is often unnecessary. It also questions the possibility of interpretable scientific discovery when prior knowledge is lacking. We believe a precise and philosophically informed definition of interpretability in SciML will help focus research efforts toward the most significant obstacles to realizing a data-driven scientific future.

papers.title: Open Problems in Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: What are the key open problems in mechanistic interpretability methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges that need to be addressed to achieve the field's goals?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes and outlines key open problems in mechanistic interpretability, covering methods, applications, and socio-technical challenges to guide future research.
papers.conclusion: The review outlines critical open problems in mechanistic interpretability that must be addressed to achieve scientific and engineering goals, emphasizing the need for methodological improvements and socio-technical integration.
papers.key_findings:
Mechanistic interpretability methods, such as sparse dictionary learning, suffer from practical and conceptual limitations like high reconstruction errors and unclear theoretical foundations.
Applying interpretability to AI safety requires robust methods for monitoring internal states and controlling behavior, but current techniques are insufficient.
Socio-technical challenges include integrating interpretability into AI governance and addressing philosophical questions about the field's goals.
future_direction: Developing better decomposition methods like sparse dictionary learning with lower reconstruction errors.
Creating validation frameworks for interpretability hypotheses.
Applying interpretability to AI safety monitoring and control.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the computational mechanisms underlying neural networks' capabilities in order to accomplish concrete scientific and engineering goals. Progress in this field thus promises to provide greater assurance over AI system behavior and shed light on exciting scientific questions about the nature of intelligence. Despite recent progress toward these goals, there are many open problems in the field that require solutions before many scientific and practical benefits can be realized: Our methods require both conceptual and practical improvements to reveal deeper insights; we must figure out how best to apply our methods in pursuit of specific goals; and the field must grapple with socio-technical challenges that influence and are influenced by our work. This forward-facing review discusses the current frontier of mechanistic interpretability and the open problems that the field may benefit from prioritizing.

papers.title: Model Interpretability through the Lens of Computational Complexity
papers.research_question: How can we formally compare the interpretability of different model classes using computational complexity theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a complexity-based framework (c-interpretability) for comparing model interpretability and proves that it aligns with folklore beliefs: linear and tree-based models are more interpretable than neural networks, and shallow networks are more interpretable than deep ones.
papers.conclusion: The complexity-based framework provides a formal correlate to folklore interpretability claims, but the authors do not claim it as the definitive notion of interpretability, which remains subjective.
papers.key_findings:
FBDDs are strictly more c-interpretable than MLPs with respect to the minimum change required (MCR), minimum sufficient reason (MSR), and count completions (CC) queries.
Perceptrons are strictly more c-interpretable than MLPs for MCR and MSR, but not for CC, where both are #P-complete.
The comparison between FBDDs and perceptrons is mixed: perceptrons are more c-interpretable for MSR, while FBDDs are more c-interpretable for CC; both are in PTIME for MCR.
Using parameterized complexity, the paper shows that shallow MLPs are more interpretable than deeper MLPs for the MCR query.
The complexity of answering explainability queries varies across model classes: for example, MCR is in PTIME for FBDDs and perceptrons but NP-complete for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In spite of several claims stating that some models are more interpretable than others -- e.g., "linear models are more interpretable than deep neural networks" -- we still lack a principled notion of interpretability to formally compare among different classes of models. We make a step towards such a notion by studying whether folklore interpretability claims have a correlate in terms of computational complexity theory. We focus on local post-hoc explainability queries that, intuitively, attempt to answer why individual inputs are classified in a certain way by a given model. In a nutshell, we say that a class $\mathcal{C}_1$ of models is more interpretable than another class $\mathcal{C}_2$, if the computational complexity of answering post-hoc queries for models in $\mathcal{C}_2$ is higher than for those in $\mathcal{C}_1$. We prove that this notion provides a good theoretical counterpart to current beliefs on the interpretability of models; in particular, we show that under our definition and assuming standard complexity-theoretical assumptions (such as P$\neq$NP), both linear and tree-based models are strictly more interpretable than neural networks. Our complexity analysis, however, does not provide a clear-cut difference between linear and tree-based models, as we obtain different results depending on the particular post-hoc explanations considered. Finally, by applying a finer complexity analysis based on parameterized complexity, we are able to prove a theoretical result suggesting that shallow neural networks are more interpretable than deeper ones.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: Relational Composition in Neural Networks: A Survey and Call to Action
papers.research_question: How do neural networks represent relational composition of features, and what are the implications for interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: This paper surveys existing mechanisms for relational composition in neural networks and argues that understanding these mechanisms is crucial for interpretability, highlighting potential issues like feature multiplicity and dark matter.
papers.conclusion: The paper advocates for continued research into relational composition mechanisms, as identifying them would advance interpretability, and even their absence would be an important theoretical result.
papers.key_findings:
Feature multiplicity may occur, where multiple distinct vectors correspond to the same concept, complicating interpretability.
Dark matter may exist, where some features or combinations are systematically hidden from standard feature identification methods.
Predict/control discrepancy may arise, where vectors for predicting network behavior differ from those for controlling it.
Relational composition mechanisms (e.g., additive matrix binding, multi-token mechanisms, vector symbolic architectures) could be present in neural networks and affect interpretability.
Understanding relational composition is essential for advancing interpretability and could help organize feature catalogs.
papers.limitation: The arguments are conjectural and often involve idealized settings.
future_direction: Toy models that learn composition.
Apply feature extraction methods to synthetic composition mechanisms.
Apply dictionary learning to token differences.
papers.abstract: Many neural nets appear to represent data as linear combinations of "feature vectors." Algorithms for discovering these vectors have seen impressive recent success. However, we argue that this success is incomplete without an understanding of relational composition: how (or whether) neural nets combine feature vectors to represent more complicated relationships. To facilitate research in this area, this paper offers a guided tour of various relational mechanisms that have been proposed, along with preliminary analysis of how such mechanisms might affect the search for interpretable features. We end with a series of promising areas for empirical research, which may help determine how neural networks represent structured data.

papers.title: Interpretability Bottleneck Breakthrough Method for Deep Learning Algorithms
papers.research_question: What are the fundamental challenges in model interpretability, and how can they be addressed through innovative methods such as self-explaining neural architectures, adaptive interpretation frameworks, and collaborative systems?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes self-explaining neural architectures, adaptive interpretation frameworks, and collaborative systems to enhance model interpretability while preserving predictive performance.
papers.conclusion: This paper investigates the core issues of interpretability in deep learning and proposes several innovative methods, including self-explaining architectures, dynamic interpretation optimization, and human-AI collaborative interpretation, which significantly enhance interpretability while preserving model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Current interpretability methods face challenges in providing meaningful explanations due to unclear semantics of learned features and limitations of explanation techniques.
Self-explaining neural architectures that generate explanations alongside predictions can enhance transparency.
Adaptive interpretation frameworks that adjust to different contexts improve interpretability.
Collaborative systems that combine AI analysis with human expertise advance trustworthy AI.
Experimental results show the proposed methods enhance model transparency while preserving predictive performance.
papers.limitation: need for improved interpretation capabilities for time-series and multimodal data, as well as further optimization of computational efficiency
future_direction: incorporating causal reasoning techniques to generate more logically sound explanations
exploring interpretability enhancement methods under privacy-preserving frameworks
establishing interdisciplinary evaluation standards
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success across various domains, yet their opaque decision-making processes hinder their deployment in critical applications such as healthcare and finance. This paper examines fundamental challenges in model interpretability, including the unclear semantics of learned features, limitations of current explanation techniques, and the inherent tension between accuracy and explainability. We analyze prevailing interpretation methods, including attention mechanisms, feature attribution approaches, and surrogate models, identifying key shortcomings in their ability to provide meaningful explanations. To address these limitations, we introduce several innovative approaches: self-explaining neural architectures that generate explanations alongside predictions, adaptive interpretation frameworks that adjust to different contexts, and collaborative systems that combine AI analysis with human expertise. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed methods significantly enhance model transparency while preserving predictive performance. These contributions advance both theoretical understanding of deep learning interpretability and practical methodologies for developing more trustworthy AI systems. The findings provide valuable insights for researchers and practitioners seeking to implement explainable AI solutions in real-world scenarios where decision accountability is paramount.

papers.title: Neurons to Words: A Novel Method for Automated Neural Network Interpretability and Alignment
papers.research_question: Can neural network activations be automatically translated into human-readable language to interpret the internal workings of the model?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a generic, scalable method for automatically interpreting neural networks by translating activations into human-readable language, demonstrated on a CNN trained on MNIST.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates the feasibility of automatically interpreting neural networks by converting activations into human-readable language, and suggests that with sufficient computational resources, the method could scale to monitor the internal mechanisms of advanced AI models.
papers.key_findings:
The method successfully translates activations of a CNN's first convolutional layer into human-readable descriptions of shapes.
Fine-tuned LLMs (Mistral7b and Mixtral8x7b) achieve high accuracy in identifying shapes from synthetic and MNIST data.
The interpreter models can generalize to unseen shapes (e.g., curves) by leveraging learned features and pre-trained knowledge.
The method loses some spatial information and granularity due to flattening and binning of activations.
Larger and more diverse datasets could improve performance and generalization.
papers.limitation:
The method loses spatial information and granularity due to flattening and binning of activations.
The 28x28 image resolution makes it hard to distinguish between round shapes and angular corners.
The structured descriptions lack linguistic diversity, making the model less flexible in generating natural language.
The fine-tuned model sometimes continues generating activations or shapes even after accurate predictions.
Computational resources limited the study to the MNIST dataset.
future_direction: Using larger and more detailed datasets to yield more informative activations.
Leveraging LLMs for natural description generation to improve linguistic diversity.
Training multiple interpreters in parallel to improve consistency and comprehensiveness.
papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed an increase in the parameter size of frontier AI models by multiple orders of magnitude. This trend is driven by empirical observations, known as scaling laws, which show that model performance scales with model size, dataset size, and computational power. Motivated by this, researchers are training ever-larger models in pursuit of unlocking new capabilities. However, the growing complexity of these models makes understanding their inner workings increasingly challenging. Interpretability is crucial not only in fields like medicine and biotechnology, where understanding the internals of these models could lead to new insights but also in super alignment, where it is the goal to ensure that AI is aligned and acts according to human values and interests. We present a generic, scalable first-of-its-kind method for automatically interpreting neural networks. In a proof-of-concept study we establish the viability of converting neural network activations - here for the first layer of a Convolutional Neural Network - into human-readable language. Additionally, we propose modifications to scale this method for understanding neural networks of any size. In anticipation of more capable large language models, this method could enable the monitoring of their internal mechanisms and decisions.

papers.title: Exploiting Latent Linearity in LLMs Improves Explainable Molecular Representation Learning
papers.research_question: Can LLM-derived molecular representations be linearly decomposed into chemically meaningful concepts (functional groups), and how can this latent linearity be exploited for explainable molecular property prediction?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MoleX, a framework that decomposes LLM latent representations into a concept-aligned space of functional groups and shows that a sparse linear mapping onto these chemical concepts improves both predictive accuracy and explainability for molecular property prediction.
